Name: Margaret Thornton
Location: Upper East Side, New York, NY
Source Content: Margaret Thornton has been a museum patron for over fifteen years and is one of the most consistently engaged major donors in the portfolio. She is a senior partner at Thornton & Lewis LLP, a boutique estate and trust law firm headquartered in Midtown Manhattan, where she has practiced for thirty years. Her collecting interest centers on post-war American painting — she has spoken at length about Cy Twombly, Robert Rauschenberg, and Jasper Johns, and attended every opening tied to that period in recent memory. She joined the Collections Advisory Committee in 2019 and has been an active, well-prepared voice in those meetings. Margaret personally introduced David Chen to the museum in early 2023 after he made partner at Thornton & Lewis; she described him as someone who was ready to start giving back and thought the Young Patrons Circle would be a natural fit for him. She attended the 2024 Spring Gala with her husband Philip. In March 2024 she met with the Director of Major Gifts over lunch at the Four Seasons; the conversation turned to endowing a conservation fellowship specifically tied to works on paper, which aligns with her Twombly focus. She has made annual gifts for fifteen consecutive years and contributed a major capital gift in 2020 toward the north wing expansion. She also serves on the board of the New York Drawing Center. Margaret prefers a formal written proposal before any solicitation; the relationship is warm and long-established. Next cultivation step is a small curator-led studio visit in fall 2024, followed by a conservation fellowship proposal in Q1 2025 targeting $750,000 over five years.

Name: David Chen
Source Content: David Chen is a junior partner at Thornton & Lewis LLP, the same firm where Margaret Thornton is a senior partner. Margaret introduced him to the museum in October 2023, and his first event was the Young Patrons Circle benefit that fall. He specializes in corporate M&A and made partner in 2022, faster than the typical track at the firm. He has since made two annual fund gifts and appears genuinely excited about the museum rather than treating giving as a professional obligation. In conversations with the membership coordinator he expressed strong interest in contemporary Asian-American artists — he mentioned collecting work by Hernan Bas and was visibly enthusiastic when he learned about the museum's recent Tschabalala Self acquisition. He is 38, lives in Tribeca, and his career trajectory suggests his giving capacity will grow significantly over the next three to five years. Outside work he is a serious marathon runner; he ran Berlin and Tokyo in 2023 and brought it up in both of his meetings with staff. He has met with the membership coordinator twice and seems ready for an introduction to a curator for a more substantive art-focused relationship. No solicitation is planned at this stage — the focus is cultivation. Best engagement angle is artist talks and the social programming around Young Patrons events, which he described as the highlight of his first year as a member.

Name: Patricia Kellner
Location: Upper West Side, New York, NY
Source Content: Patricia Kellner is a retired Managing Director from Goldman Sachs, where she spent twenty-two years running the private wealth management division before leaving in 2018. She lives on the Upper West Side with her husband Robert Kellner, who is also a museum donor. She is a serious collector with several works by Jean-Michel Basquiat and Kerry James Marshall acquired both privately and through the museum's benefit auctions over the years. Patricia served two terms on the museum's Board of Trustees from 2015 to 2021 and stepped back deliberately to focus on her personal philanthropic portfolio. She now chairs the Kellner Family Foundation, which supports arts education programming at five New York nonprofits. She and Robert have attended every gala in recent memory as a couple. In a March 2024 conversation with the Executive Director she expressed pointed frustration that the museum has leaned too heavily into digital and NFT programming at the expense of exhibitions focused on traditional media — this is a real sensitivity to flag for any curator or program officer who interacts with her. She has discussed including the museum in her estate plan and the conversation about a major bequest is ongoing; her estate attorney handles the details, and there is reason to believe that attorney may be at Thornton & Lewis, though this has not been confirmed. Next step is an invitation to preview the fall painting survey exhibition before its public opening, which would directly address her concern about traditional media being prioritized.

Name: Robert Kellner
Location: Upper West Side, New York, NY
Source Content: Robert Kellner is a principal architect and co-founder of Kellner Maier Architects, a mid-size firm with a strong portfolio in cultural and civic buildings. He is married to Patricia Kellner, who is also a museum donor. His engagement with the museum is as much architectural as philanthropic — he has an active and informed perspective on the planned south gallery expansion and met twice in 2023 with the Deputy Director for Capital Projects to offer informal design input. His contributions in those conversations were substantive and he offered them entirely pro bono. His personal collecting focus is architectural drawings and fine art photography; he has spoken warmly about Stephen Shore and Andreas Gursky and has attended several photography-focused programming events independently of Patricia. He and Patricia fly to Basel for Art Basel every year. He attended a solo curator talk on the new photography wing in January 2024, which was unusual since he rarely participates in programming without her. His firm has completed building projects for two other New York cultural institutions. A formal acknowledgment of his architectural engagement — perhaps a behind-the-scenes briefing with the capital team on expansion planning — would deepen the relationship and could open a path to either a capital campaign gift or a formal design partnership as the south gallery project advances.

Name: Roland Jeffers
Source Content: Roland Jeffers is a managing director in private wealth management at Goldman Sachs, serving ultra-high-net-worth clients across the arts and entertainment industry. He has spent his entire career at the firm after graduating from Georgetown, where he studied philosophy. Roland and his partner live in a renovated apartment in Fort Greene, Brooklyn, close to Brooklyn Academy of Music, which they attend several times a month. His personal collecting is focused on Basquiat-era work and its contemporaries — he owns a Keith Haring canvas and has recently acquired a Kerry James Marshall print through the museum's benefit auction. He attended Art Basel Miami last December as both a client host and a personal collector and described the experience as the most productive fair he'd attended in years. He is active in the Jazz at Lincoln Center patron community and serves on the advisory board of the New Museum. Michael Torres manages the relationship. Roland is well-connected and a natural peer-introducer; consider engaging him in a museum collector's advisory group.

Name: Oliver Ashford
Source Content: Oliver Ashford retired three years ago from a thirty-year career at Bain & Company, where he rose to senior partner leading the firm's private equity advisory group. He and his wife Frances, a landscape architect, split their time between a townhouse in the West Village and a sailing compound in Newport, Rhode Island. Oliver has competed in the Newport-Bermuda Race four times aboard his 52-foot sloop Albatross and is active in the New York Yacht Club. His collecting interests are eclectic: he began with Abstract Expressionism in the 1990s and has since expanded into contemporary figuration, particularly painters from the UK. He owns a Peter Doig print and has been in dialogue with Christie's about a Cecily Brown works-on-paper piece. Oliver serves on the board of the Public Art Fund and has been an informal advisor to the museum's executive director on strategic planning questions. James Reuter manages the relationship and reports that Oliver has expressed curiosity about establishing a named endowment to support the museum's contemporary acquisitions fund. Cultivation priority: private dinner with the director and chief curator. Major gift potential.

Name: Tanisha Brooks
Source Content: Tanisha Brooks is a documentary photographer and visual journalist whose work has been exhibited at the International Center of Photography, the Aperture Gallery, and several international festivals. She spent five years on assignment for a major wire service before transitioning to long-form documentary projects focused on Black maternal health and intergenerational poverty in the rural South. Tanisha lives in Bedford-Stuyvesant and was introduced to the museum through an artist residency program three years ago. She has since become a vocal advocate for the museum's community access programming and has sat on two panels organized by the education department. Her giving is modest — $1,500 annually — but she actively refers potential donors and has made introductions to three individuals who became members. Sarah Okafor manages the relationship and considers her a high-value community ambassador regardless of giving level. Recommend giving her a meaningful advisory role, such as community programming committee, to reflect her actual contribution to the museum's network.

Name: Celeste Fontaine-Ward
Source Content: Celeste Fontaine-Ward is a curatorial fellow turned independent curator based in Bushwick, who organizes exhibitions out of an artist-run space she co-founded four years ago. She completed her MA in curatorial studies at Bard CCS after undergraduate work at Howard University. Her giving is symbolic — $750 annually — but her role in the Bushwick Open Studios network and her relationships with a dozen artists who will matter to institutions within five years make her a priority cultivation target. She was introduced to the museum by Diana Flores after meeting at an artist residency studio visit. Celeste is deeply knowledgeable about photography and post-internet art, and she has consulted informally with the museum's assistant curator on two occasions. She runs most mornings in Maria Hernandez Park and describes it as her only form of meditation. Michael Torres has begun accompanying Diana Flores on cultivation meetings to help broaden the relationship team's connection to the Bushwick scene. Annual gift; recommend involving her in community advisory programming.

Name: Constance Ellory
Source Content: Constance Ellory is a retired pediatric cardiologist who practiced at Children's Hospital of Philadelphia for thirty years before retiring to a penthouse in the West Village she purchased in 2019. She was widowed six years ago; her late husband was a sculptor, and the apartment contains a significant group of his work alongside photographs and ceramics she has collected independently. Constance has deep ties to the Philadelphia art world through her late husband's career, and she is building new relationships in New York with considerable deliberateness. She has attended the museum's medical community membership events twice and has engaged in extended conversation with the photography curator about a group of archival prints by her husband she is considering placing on long-term loan. Priya Mehta manages the relationship with sensitivity and care. Constance has mentioned a potential bequest several times in passing; the planned giving office should be introduced in a low-key context. Annual gift currently $4,500; mid-tier trajectory. Long-term planned gift potential is significant.

Name: Devon St. Claire
Source Content: Devon St. Claire is an emerging fashion stylist and creative consultant whose clients include several major music artists and a roster of editorial clients at Vogue and Harper's Bazaar. He grew up in Flatbush, studied fashion design at Pratt, and built his practice over seven years of relentless freelancing. Devon lives in a carefully appointed studio apartment in Prospect Heights. His art interest is vivid and associative — he gravitates toward photography that engages with fashion, performance, and Black cultural expression — and he owns prints by Hype Williams stills and documentary photographers he discovered through social media. He was introduced to the museum by Tanisha Brooks at an ICP event and has attended three openings since. His annual giving is $1,000 but he brings energy, connections, and a social media presence to every event he attends. Sarah Okafor manages the relationship and notes he is an important voice for the museum among a younger creative class. Recommend including him in a curatorial social media collaboration.

Name: Miriam Goldstein-Farber
Source Content: Miriam Goldstein-Farber is a retired professor of art history at Columbia University, where she taught for thirty-three years and chaired the department for a decade. She is a recognized scholar of Abstract Expressionism, having published two monographs on Lee Krasner and co-edited a volume on Clyfford Still. She lives in a large apartment near campus in Morningside Heights and has been a museum friend since the 1990s. Her giving has been at the annual level for most of her career but increased meaningfully after selling her upstate house in 2021. She attended last year's symposium on postwar American painting and gave an informal talk to staff at the curator's invitation. Miriam has mentioned to James Reuter that she is thinking about her estate and would like her collection — which includes significant prints and drawings by Motherwell and de Kooning — to eventually benefit an institution she loves. A formal planned giving conversation has not yet taken place; this should be prioritized in 2026. She has a gentle but firm personality and dislikes what she calls 'transactional' cultivation. James should approach the estate conversation through the lens of legacy and scholarship. Potential: transformative bequest.

Name: Catherine Osei-Bonsu
Source Content: Catherine Osei-Bonsu is a senior vice president in Goldman Sachs's private equity group, focusing on healthcare and life sciences investments. She completed her MBA at Columbia Business School and joined GS directly after. She lives in Park Slope with her husband, an architect, and their infant daughter. Catherine is a serious collector for her age — she has been building a collection around Abstract Expressionism for six years, owning two Lee Krasner paintings and a Clyfford Still work on paper. She attended the museum's Abstract Expressionism spring preview and requested a follow-up meeting with the curator, which took place in April. She is a member of the Guggenheim Foundation's junior council. Priya Mehta manages the relationship; Catherine upgraded from annual to mid-tier this year after the curator meeting. She is ambitious professionally and is on a trajectory that suggests capacity well above current giving level within five years. Cultivation priority: develop peer relationship with curator, not just development staff.

Name: Konstantin Petrov
Location: Upper East Side, New York, NY
Source Content: Konstantin Petrov is a managing director at a European investment bank's structured finance division in Midtown, where he specializes in securitization and covered bond markets. He trained as an economist at Moscow State University before a master's at LSE and has lived in New York for fourteen years. He and his wife Natasha live in a pre-war apartment on the Upper East Side. Konstantin collects photography with a European collector's eye — he has a Wolfgang Tillmans large-format print, a Gursky offset work acquired at Art Basel Miami Beach two years ago, and a vintage Richard Avedon fashion photograph discovered at a Paris flea market. He attended Art Basel in Basel last June for the sixth time. He joined the museum's Patron Circle at the invitation of a banking colleague and has given $10,000 annually for the past three years. Diana Flores manages his account and notes that he is punctual, organized, and responds to cultivation that respects his time. Next steps: propose a three-year pledge at $15,000 annually to the photography endowment. He is ready to move up.

Name: Eleanor Strand
Source Content: Eleanor Strand is a retired principal at Morgan Stanley where she spent thirty-one years in wealth management, ultimately running the New York private wealth division. She and her husband Walter, a retired architect, live in a townhouse in Brooklyn Heights and spend summers in Watch Hill, Rhode Island. Eleanor has been a museum trustee for eleven years and is currently vice chair of the collections committee. Her personal collection focuses on photography — she owns twenty-three major prints spanning from Diane Arbus to Wolfgang Tillmans and lends regularly to the museum's special exhibitions. She attended Art Basel Basel last June and made two significant purchases. Eleanor's family foundation, the Strand-Hollis Foundation, has given over $1.2 million to the museum cumulatively, including the endowed Strand Photography Study Room. Michael Torres manages the relationship with great care; current cultivation is focused on a potential capital campaign gift in the $1 million range for the planned new wing.

Name: Sophie Marchetti
Source Content: Sophie Marchetti is a creative director at a luxury fashion house, Velours Maison, based in Midtown. Before moving to New York she spent twelve years in Milan working for two major Italian labels in visual identity and runway direction. At 48 she has a sophisticated eye and a well-edited collection centered on contemporary photography — she owns three Richard Avedon prints, a Wolfgang Tillmans, and a Cindy Sherman from the Society Portraits series. She attended Frieze New York last spring and Art Basel Miami Beach in December, buying at both. She lives in SoHo and is part of a collector social circle that overlaps with several other museum donors. Sophie has agreed to host a small private salon at her apartment for the museum's photography curator next spring — this is a significant cultivation event and coordination should begin in November. James Reuter manages the relationship. She is personally generous and socially influential; a peer-influence strategy is appropriate. Current annual giving $6,000; mid-level step-up conversation is timely.

Name: Ben Shapiro-Levi
Source Content: Ben Shapiro-Levi is a 33-year-old associate at a boutique impact investment fund focused on climate and regenerative agriculture. He holds an MPP from Harvard Kennedy School and previously worked at the Rockefeller Brothers Fund. He lives in Bed-Stuy, Brooklyn, and is part of a younger arts community there — he helped organize a pop-up exhibition of emerging artists in a repurposed warehouse last summer. His personal collecting leans toward contemporary photography: he owns prints by Nan Goldin and an early Wolfgang Tillmans bought at a benefit auction. He is a marathon runner who completed the NYC Marathon and is registered for the Boston Marathon. He attended Frieze New York with a friend who is a gallerist and found it energizing. Diana Flores manages the relationship and should introduce him to the museum's emerging collector circle, which is the most appropriate cultivation vehicle at this stage. Annual gift $1,200; peer community cultivation is the strategy. Mid-level potential in five to seven years.

Name: Miriam Goldstein-Levy
Location: Upper West Side, New York, NY
Source Content: Miriam Goldstein-Levy is the president of the Goldstein Family Foundation, a $180-million vehicle that supports arts, public health, and education. She is 63 and lives on the Upper West Side with her husband, a retired oncologist. She served for years on the board of the New York Philharmonic and currently chairs its endowment committee. The foundation has been a museum institutional supporter for twelve years, but her personal donor relationship is only three years old. Her collecting is centered on Abstract Expressionism — she owns a major de Kooning painting that she has lent to the museum twice — and Minimalism, particularly Agnes Martin. She attended Art Basel Basel in June, as she does most years. James Reuter manages the foundation relationship; Michael Torres manages the personal relationship. The two streams should be coordinated carefully to avoid duplication of asks. A joint foundation-personal commitment at the major level is the goal; initial conversation indicated appetite for a named gallery in the new east wing. Current personal giving $50,000; foundation annual grant $75,000.

Name: Ifeoma Chukwuemeka
Source Content: Ifeoma Chukwuemeka is a 40-year-old senior associate at Weil, Gotshal & Manges, specializing in private equity fund formation and investment management regulation. Born in Onitsha, Nigeria, and raised in London, she attended Queen Mary University of London and Columbia Law School. She has been in New York for eight years and lives in Fort Greene, Brooklyn. Ifeoma's museum engagement began through a professional women's network that organized a members preview event at the museum two years ago. Her collecting interests are in contemporary African photography — she owns prints by Zanele Muholi and Malick Sidibé, and follows the work of Seun Akisanmi closely. She attended Frieze London last October while visiting family. Michael Torres manages the relationship. She is an annual-level donor and has been responsive and engaged; attending four or five programs per year. Her Weil Gotshal connection overlaps with the estate attorney mentioned for another major donor in the portfolio — an interesting coincidence that should not affect their separate relationship management. A mid-tier cultivation conversation is appropriate in the next twelve months, with the African photography acquisitions fund as the natural focus. She is also a USTA tennis player — competes in a doubles league in Brooklyn on weekends.

Name: Viktor Breckenridge
Source Content: Viktor Breckenridge is a 70-year-old retired publishing executive who served as CEO of a major academic press for eighteen years before retiring in 2019. He grew up in Chicago, studied English at the University of Chicago, and spent his career in New York. He lives in the West Village with his partner, a retired journalist. Viktor has been a museum member since 1985 and a major donor since 2004. His collection is broad and deeply personal — he has a Franz Kline large canvas, a Rothko study, three de Kooning Women lithographs, and a strong group of figurative works including a Lucian Freud etching and an Alice Neel portrait. He attended Art Basel Basel annually for fifteen years, stopping in 2022 due to a hip replacement. He serves as a trustee of the Dia Art Foundation and is a longtime member of the Century Association. Priya Mehta manages the museum relationship. Viktor's giving has been steady at the major tier for twenty years. His estate plan includes a bequest of a portion of the collection, with negotiation ongoing regarding which works. The key next step is a private meeting with the director and chief curator to discuss collection succession — Viktor wants to ensure works go where they will be studied, not stored.

Name: Margaret Chen
Source Content: Margaret Chen is a senior partner at Cravath Swaine & Moore in their litigation practice, specializing in securities fraud defense. She graduated from Harvard Law and clerked for Judge Rakoff in the Southern District. She lives in a townhouse in the West Village with her partner and their rescue greyhound. Margaret is a keen collector of Abstract Expressionism and has acquired works on paper by Lee Krasner and a small de Kooning sketch that she discovered at a regional auction in 2017. She attends Art Basel Basel each year, typically with a buying budget in the high five figures, and has attended Frieze London twice in the past three years. She sits on the board of the Dia Art Foundation, where she chairs the legal affairs subcommittee. The museum was introduced to her by Dia's executive director. She attended our de Kooning study day last April and spoke admiringly about the works-on-paper holdings. James has the relationship. Next step: invite her to the curator's private dinner in February. Long-term ask potential of $50,000 toward the endowment is realistic within two years.

Name: Isabel Ferreira
Source Content: Isabel Ferreira is a 33-year-old digital product manager at a major streaming platform, where she leads the platform's arts and culture vertical. She grew up in São Paulo in a family with strong ties to the Brazilian art world — her mother was a gallerist — and moved to New York for college at NYU. She now lives in Astoria, Queens. Her collection is emerging and reflects her dual heritage: she has acquired works by young Brazilian Neo-Expressionist painters and one photograph by Nan Goldin purchased at a benefit auction. She attended Frieze New York in May and spent time with galleries representing Latin American artists. She discovered our museum through a digital collaboration proposal she submitted that the education team responded to enthusiastically. She has since made her first gift of $750 and attended one member event. Sarah should nurture this relationship through digital engagement programming and collaborative content opportunities. Long-term potential is strong given her platform and her family's background. No family foundation yet. Annual ask: $1,000.

Name: Priya Chandrasekaran
Source Content: Priya Chandrasekaran is a 40-year-old partner at Davis Polk & Wardwell, specializing in leveraged finance and capital markets. She grew up in Scarsdale, New York, attended Yale, and completed her JD at NYU Law. She commutes to Midtown from her home in Scarsdale, where she lives with her husband and two children. She is a competitive club tennis player, competing in USTA league play and the Scarsdale Golf & Country Club's annual tournament. Her art interest is relatively new — sparked by a visit to Art Basel Miami three years ago with a client — but has developed rapidly. She has acquired two photographs by Andreas Gursky and a work on paper by Cindy Sherman. She attended our photography benefit in September as a guest of Margaret Chen and responded enthusiastically. She has since joined as a new donor at the mid level. Priya (the RM) should schedule a studio visit to the photography collection with her in the coming months. She has mentioned potential interest in serving on a junior advisory board. Ask for next cycle: $10,000.

Name: Neha Patel
Source Content: Neha Patel is a 39-year-old co-founder of a Series C health-tech startup, having previously worked in product management at Google and completed an undergraduate degree in computer science at Stanford. She was born in Ahmedabad, India, and grew up in the Bay Area before moving to New York to launch her company. She lives in a loft in Williamsburg with her husband, a documentary filmmaker. She is new to collecting but has developed a genuine and fast-moving interest: she owns two photographs by Andreas Gursky and recently acquired a Cindy Sherman film still. She attended Art Basel Miami for the first time this December and described it as transformative. She is not yet a museum donor but attended a young patron event as a guest of Isabel Ferreira and expressed strong interest in joining the giving circle. Sarah should follow up promptly with membership materials. Neha has a broad network among tech and startup founders in New York who represent an underserved donor demographic for the museum. Her husband's documentary film work creates a natural bridge to photography programming. Annual ask to start: $3,000.

Name: Sunita Bhattacharya
Source Content: Sunita Bhattacharya is chief marketing officer at a luxury fashion house with North American headquarters in Midtown. She previously held senior brand roles at LVMH and Kering. She lives in a light-filled apartment in the West Village that she has decorated with a mix of fashion photography and contemporary works. Her collecting interests center on photography — she owns prints by Nan Goldin and Wolfgang Tillmans and has been in conversations with a gallery about a significant Andreas Gursky photograph. She attended both Frieze New York and Frieze London this year and is a regular at Art Basel Miami Beach. Sunita has been on the museum's fashion and culture advisory circle since it launched two years ago and contributed meaningfully to the planning of a recent exhibition on dress and identity. She is a recreational tennis player, competing in club-level doubles at the Village Tennis Club. Annual fund ask of $4,000, with a note to explore mid-level engagement as her role and compensation have grown significantly in the past two years.

Name: Priscilla Huang-Ashworth
Source Content: Priscilla Huang-Ashworth is a principal at a Chicago-based architecture firm with an active New York office. She splits her time between Chicago and a rental in the West Village, spending roughly half her year in each city. Her collecting interest is Minimalism — she owns works by Dan Flavin and Anne Truitt and has been in a two-year conversation with a dealer about a Donald Judd stack piece. She attended Art Basel Miami Beach this past December and met with the museum's curatorial director, who was there with the acquisitions committee. She is a member of the advisory council of the Art Institute of Chicago and gives to both institutions. Her relationship manager notes a potential tension: she has expressed mild frustration that the museum's programming seems centered on New York donors and that Chicago-based collectors are not given equivalent access to preview events — a sensitivity worth addressing with a dedicated invitation to the next private view. Mid-level ask of $12,000; resolving the geographic accessibility friction is a prerequisite.

Name: Eleanor Whitfield-Cross
Location: Upper West Side, New York, NY
Source Content: Eleanor Whitfield-Cross retired five years ago as Chief Investment Officer of a mid-size family office after a long career that began in fixed income at Vanguard, where she spent a decade before moving to the private side. She and her late husband Arthur endowed a small foundation, the Whitfield-Cross Family Foundation, which focuses on arts education and environmental preservation. Eleanor lives alone now in a large apartment on the Upper West Side; her adult children are in Boston and San Francisco. She is a long-standing museum trustee emerita and has been in a preliminary bequest conversation with the development office — legal counsel has been looped in and an estate planning meeting is scheduled for September. Her collecting interests are in Minimalism: she owns several Donald Judd stack pieces and an Agnes Martin drawing that she regards as among her most treasured possessions. Eleanor attended Art Basel Basel twice in the 1990s and once more in 2019. Diana Flores manages the relationship with great sensitivity; the planned giving discussion should proceed at Eleanor's pace without pressure.

Name: David Okonkwo
Location: Upper East Side, New York, NY
Source Content: David Okonkwo is a managing partner at a mid-size private equity firm in Midtown, focusing on healthcare and life sciences buyouts. He spent a decade at Goldman Sachs in the Healthcare Investment Banking group before co-founding his current firm. David and his wife Adaeze live on the Upper East Side and are active in the Nigerian-American professional community in New York. His collecting interests lie in Basquiat, Kerry James Marshall, and works by emerging Black artists he has been buying through galleries in Bed-Stuy and Harlem. He attended the museum's opening for the recent contemporary African American art exhibition and donated to the accompanying catalogue. David is a committed marathon runner — he completed the Boston Marathon this year in 3:28 after training through the winter. Priya Mehta has been building the relationship steadily; he gave $10,000 last fiscal year and there is capacity for considerably more. A $50,000 major gift conversation focused on a named acquisition fund is planned for Q3.

Name: Judith Rosenzweig-Kaplan
Location: Upper West Side, New York, NY
Source Content: Judith Rosenzweig-Kaplan is a retired psychiatrist and psychoanalyst who practiced in Manhattan for thirty-five years. She and her husband Arnold, a retired professor of philosophy, live in Riverside Drive in an apartment that doubles as a small private museum. Her collecting interests are in Abstract Expressionism and the New York School — she owns works by Lee Krasner, Robert Motherwell, and a Pollock ink drawing she acquired in the 1970s through a gallery friendship. She has been a museum patron for decades and gave to the building campaign in the 1990s. Judith and Arnold established the Rosenzweig-Kaplan Foundation in 2008, supporting psychoanalytic education and the arts. She has been in a quiet bequest conversation with the development office for two years; the estate attorney has confirmed that the museum is named as a beneficiary for a portion of the collection as well as a financial bequest. Diana Flores manages the relationship at the highest priority level. Annual giving is at the major level, $60,000 last year. No pressure; this is a lifelong relationship.

Name: Svetlana Volkov-Reiss
Source Content: Svetlana Volkov-Reiss is a fashion and luxury consultant who spent fifteen years as a senior executive at LVMH before launching her own advisory practice serving European fashion houses entering the US market. She lives in SoHo and travels extensively to Paris and Milan. Her collecting centers on contemporary photography, especially Andreas Gursky's large-format works and Wolfgang Tillmans's intimate prints; she owns four Tillmans works and attended his retrospective opening at this museum last year. Svetlana attended Frieze London last October and met the curatorial team for drinks during the fair. She is 48 and donates at the mid level, having stepped up from annual giving three years ago. She supports the New Museum and sits on a young patrons committee there. Cultivation note: Svetlana has expressed interest in sponsoring a photography acquisition — Diana Flores should explore a named fund at the $30,000 entry point. She prefers email communication and responds quickly. No friction notes on file.

Name: Thomas Kimani
Source Content: Thomas Kimani is a 48-year-old chief medical officer at a mid-size pharmaceutical company, Orexa Biologics, based in New Jersey. He trained as a physician at the University of Nairobi and then completed residency and an MBA at the University of Michigan. Thomas and his wife Wanjiru live in Montclair, New Jersey, and attend museum events regularly — they make the trip into the city three or four times a year for openings. He is a mid-level donor who first gave eight years ago after attending a benefit dinner with a colleague. His collecting interest has evolved toward figurative painting and contemporary African art — he owns three works by Njideka Akunyili Crosby and has expressed interest in acquiring a Lucian Freud print. He attended Art Basel Miami in December for the first time. Priya Mehta manages the relationship. Cultivation note: Thomas is warm and engaged; his giving is personal and values-driven. He and Wanjiru would benefit from a personal welcome from the director at the next event they attend. A $20,000 pledge upgrade is a reasonable next step.
